BCG vaccine and tuberculosis: 13 randomised trials

Author

Dr Gurpreet

Published

November 18, 2026

1 Why this dataset?

dat.bcg (Colditz et al., Clin Infect Dis 1994) ships with metafor. It has 13 trials of BCG vaccination against tuberculosis, a binary outcome, and a lot of heterogeneity with a plausible explanation (distance from the equator). That makes it ideal for teaching every step: pooling, heterogeneity, small-study effects and sensitivity analysis.

Code 
library(metafor)
library(tidyverse)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

# Helper: metafor output -> tibble with snake_case names (ci.lb -> ci_lb)
tidy_mf <- \(x) x |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  rename_with(\(nm) str_replace_all(nm, "\\.", "_"))

2 The data

Code 
bcg <- dat.bcg |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(
    study  = str_c(author, ", ", year),
    n_vacc = tpos + tneg,
    n_ctrl = cpos + cneg
  ) |>
  select(trial, study, year, ablat, alloc,
         tpos, n_vacc, cpos, n_ctrl, tneg, cneg)

bcg |> select(study, ablat, alloc, tpos, n_vacc, cpos, n_ctrl)

tpos/cpos are TB cases in the vaccinated and control arms; ablat is the absolute latitude of the trial site.

3 Step 1: Effect size for each study

escalc() computes the log risk ratio (yi) and its sampling variance (vi). We analyse on the log scale and back-transform for reporting.

Code 
bcg_es <- escalc(
  measure = "RR",
  ai = tpos, bi = tneg,   # vaccinated: events, non-events
  ci = cpos, di = cneg,   # control:    events, non-events
  data = bcg,
  slab = study
)

bcg_es |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(
    rr    = exp(yi),
    lower = exp(yi - 1.96 * sqrt(vi)),
    upper = exp(yi + 1.96 * sqrt(vi))
  ) |>
  select(study, yi, vi, rr, lower, upper) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
study yi vi rr lower upper
Aronson, 1948 -0.889 0.326 0.411 0.134 1.257
Ferguson & Simes, 1949 -1.585 0.195 0.205 0.086 0.486
Rosenthal et al, 1960 -1.348 0.415 0.260 0.073 0.919
Hart & Sutherland, 1977 -1.442 0.020 0.237 0.179 0.312
Frimodt-Moller et al, 1973 -0.218 0.051 0.804 0.516 1.254
Stein & Aronson, 1953 -0.786 0.007 0.456 0.387 0.536
Vandiviere et al, 1973 -1.621 0.223 0.198 0.078 0.499
TPT Madras, 1980 0.012 0.004 1.012 0.895 1.145

4 Step 2: Pool the studies

Code 
res_fe <- rma(yi, vi, data = bcg_es, method = "EE")    # common (fixed) effect
res_re <- rma(yi, vi, data = bcg_es, method = "REML")  # random effects

res_re

Random-Effects Model (k = 13; tau^2 estimator: REML)

tau^2 (estimated amount of total heterogeneity): 0.3132 (SE = 0.1664)
tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):      0.5597
I^2 (total heterogeneity / total variability):   92.22%
H^2 (total variability / sampling variability):  12.86

Test for Heterogeneity:
Q(df = 12) = 152.2330, p-val < .0001

Model Results:

estimate      se     zval    pval    ci.lb    ci.ub      
 -0.7145  0.1798  -3.9744  <.0001  -1.0669  -0.3622  *** 

---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
Code 
pooled <- bind_rows(
  `Common effect`  = predict(res_fe, transf = exp) |> tidy_mf(),
  `Random effects` = predict(res_re, transf = exp) |> tidy_mf(),
  .id = "model"
) |>
  select(model, rr = pred, ci_lb, ci_ub, pi_lb, pi_ub)

pooled |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))
model rr ci_lb ci_ub pi_lb pi_ub
Common effect 0.65 0.60 0.7 NA NA
Random effects 0.49 0.34 0.7 0.15 1.55
NoteReading it

Under the random-effects model, BCG vaccination is associated with a pooled RR of 0.49 (95% CI 0.34 to 0.70), roughly a 51% reduction in TB risk. The common-effect model gives a narrower and different answer because it ignores between-study variation. Here that assumption is clearly wrong (see Step 4).

5 Step 3: Forest plot

Code 
forest(
  res_re,
  atransf   = exp,
  at        = log(c(0.05, 0.25, 1, 4)),
  xlim      = c(-16, 6),
  ilab      = cbind(bcg$tpos, bcg$n_vacc, bcg$cpos, bcg$n_ctrl),
  ilab.xpos = c(-9.5, -8, -6, -4.5),
  header    = c("Study", "RR [95% CI]"),
  addpred   = TRUE,
  shade     = TRUE,
  mlab      = "Random-effects model (REML)"
)
text(c(-9.5, -8, -6, -4.5), res_re$k + 2, c("TB+", "N", "TB+", "N"), font = 2, cex = 0.8)
text(c(-8.75, -5.25),       res_re$k + 3, c("Vaccinated", "Control"), font = 2, cex = 0.8)
TipHow to read this plot
  • Each row is one study. The square is that study’s RR; the horizontal line is its 95% CI. An arrow means the CI runs off the scale.
  • Square size = weight in the pooled analysis. Big squares pull the diamond towards themselves.
  • Vertical line at RR = 1 is the line of no effect. Left of it favours vaccination (fewer TB cases); right of it favours control.
  • The diamond is the pooled RR: its centre is the point estimate and its width is the 95% CI.
  • The dotted line through the diamond is the 95% prediction interval: the range in which the true effect of a new similar study is expected to lie.
  • The x-axis is logarithmic, so RR 0.5 and RR 2 are equally far from 1.
NoteWhat we infer from it
  • Direction: 11 of 13 trials lie left of 1; only TPT Madras (RR 1.01) and Comstock & Webster (RR 1.56) do not.
  • Precision varies: 5 trials have a CI that crosses 1 on their own, yet the pooled diamond (0.49, 0.34 to 0.70) sits clearly left of 1. Pooling gives a precise answer that no single small trial could.
  • Visible heterogeneity (eyeball test): many CIs do not overlap each other (e.g. Hart & Sutherland 0.24 vs TPT Madras 1.01). Studies are not estimating one common effect.
  • Weights are fairly even (3.82% to 10.19%) because τ² is large. Under a common-effect model TPT Madras alone would carry 41.40% of the weight, versus 10.19% here.
  • Prediction interval crosses 1 (0.15 to 1.55): BCG works on average, but in some settings it may give little or no protection. Report both the CI and the PI.

6 Step 4: Heterogeneity

Code 
tibble(
  statistic = c("Q", "df", "p (Q)", "tau^2", "tau", "I^2 (%)", "H^2"),
  value     = c(res_re$QE, res_re$k - 1, res_re$QEp,
                res_re$tau2, sqrt(res_re$tau2), res_re$I2, res_re$H2)
) |>
  mutate(value = if_else(statistic == "p (Q)",
                         format.pval(value, eps = 1e-4),
                         as.character(round(value, 2))))
statistic value
Q 152.23
df 12
p (Q) < 1e-04
tau^2 0.31
tau 0.56
I^2 (%) 92.22
H^2 12.86

Confidence intervals for the heterogeneity parameters:

Code 
confint(res_re)

       estimate   ci.lb   ci.ub 
tau^2    0.3132  0.1197  1.1115 
tau      0.5597  0.3460  1.0543 
I^2(%)  92.2214 81.9177 97.6781 
H^2     12.8558  5.5303 43.0680
ImportantReading it
  • Q test: rejects homogeneity (p < 0.0001), but it has low power with few studies and too much power with many, so do not rely on it alone.
  • I² = 92%: the share of total variability due to real differences between studies, not chance. It is a proportion, not an absolute amount.
  • τ² = 0.31: the absolute between-study variance on the log RR scale.
  • Prediction interval 0.15 to 1.55: a new trial in a new setting could plausibly find anything from a large benefit to no benefit or even harm. This is often the most useful number for clinicians.

6.1 Explaining heterogeneity: meta-regression on latitude

Code 
res_mr <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ ablat, data = bcg_es, method = "REML")
res_mr

Mixed-Effects Model (k = 13; tau^2 estimator: REML)

tau^2 (estimated amount of residual heterogeneity):     0.0764 (SE = 0.0591)
tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):             0.2763
I^2 (residual heterogeneity / unaccounted variability): 68.39%
H^2 (unaccounted variability / sampling variability):   3.16
R^2 (amount of heterogeneity accounted for):            75.62%

Test for Residual Heterogeneity:
QE(df = 11) = 30.7331, p-val = 0.0012

Test of Moderators (coefficient 2):
QM(df = 1) = 16.3571, p-val < .0001

Model Results:

         estimate      se     zval    pval    ci.lb    ci.ub      
intrcpt    0.2515  0.2491   1.0095  0.3127  -0.2368   0.7397      
ablat     -0.0291  0.0072  -4.0444  <.0001  -0.0432  -0.0150  *** 

---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
Code 
lat_grid <- tibble(ablat = seq(10, 60, by = 1))

lat_pred <- predict(res_mr, newmods = lat_grid$ablat, transf = exp) |>
  tidy_mf() |>
  bind_cols(lat_grid)

bcg_es |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(rr = exp(yi), weight = 1 / vi) |>
  ggplot(aes(ablat, rr)) +
  geom_ribbon(data = lat_pred, aes(y = pred, ymin = ci_lb, ymax = ci_ub),
              fill = "grey85") +
  geom_line(data = lat_pred, aes(y = pred), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(size = weight), shape = 21, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 12, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Absolute latitude (degrees)", y = "Risk ratio (log scale)",
       subtitle = "Point size proportional to inverse-variance weight")
TipHow to read this plot
  • Each bubble is one trial, placed at its latitude (x) and its RR (y, log scale). Bubble size = weight in the meta-regression.
  • The solid line is the fitted meta-regression; the grey band is its 95% CI.
  • Dashed line at RR = 1 is no effect. Where the band sits below it, the model predicts a protective effect.
  • A sloping line means the moderator explains part of the heterogeneity; a flat line means it does not.
NoteWhat we infer from it
  • Clear dose-response with latitude: each extra degree from the equator multiplies the RR by 0.97, i.e. about 2.9% more protection per degree (p < 0.0001).
  • Near the equator BCG shows little effect (trials at 13-19°, such as TPT Madras and Frimodt-Moller, sit near RR = 1). Far from the equator it is highly protective (RR around 0.2-0.3 above 50°).
  • Latitude explains about 76% of the between-study variance (R²), and residual I² falls from 92% to 68%. Heterogeneity is largely explained, not just noise.
  • Caution: this is an observational association across studies (ecological). Latitude is a proxy for something else, plausibly prior exposure to environmental mycobacteria. With 13 studies, one moderator is the most the data can support (about 10 studies per covariate).

7 Step 5: Funnel plot

Code 
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
funnel(res_re, atransf = exp, xlab = "Risk ratio (log scale)")
funnel(res_re, level = c(90, 95, 99),
       shade = c("white", "grey80", "grey60"),
       refline = 0, legend = TRUE,
       atransf = exp, xlab = "Risk ratio (log scale)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
TipHow to read this plot
  • x-axis: each study’s effect (RR, log scale). y-axis: its standard error, inverted, so large precise studies are at the top and small imprecise ones at the bottom.
  • Vertical line: the pooled estimate. Triangle (left panel): where 95% of studies should fall if there were no bias and no heterogeneity.
  • Expected shape: a symmetrical inverted funnel. Big studies cluster tightly near the top; small studies scatter widely but evenly on both sides at the bottom.
  • Asymmetry (a gap in one bottom corner) suggests small studies with “unfavourable” results are missing.
  • Contour-enhanced panel (right): the reference line is RR = 1 and the shading marks where results are statistically significant (grey zones: p < 0.10, < 0.05, < 0.01). If the gap is in the white (non-significant) zone, publication bias is a plausible cause. If it is in a significant zone, look for other causes (heterogeneity, small-trial quality, chance).
NoteWhat we infer from it
  • The large trials (TPT Madras, Stein & Aronson, Comstock 1974, Hart & Sutherland) sit at the top but are spread widely left to right. That spread among precise studies is heterogeneity, not publication bias.
  • Many points fall outside the triangle. Expected when I² is 92%: the triangle assumes a single common effect.
  • Small trials at the bottom mostly lie to the left (strong benefit), with one on the right (Comstock & Webster, RR 1.56). There is only a mild hint of asymmetry.
  • In the contour panel, the small trials sit in both shaded and white zones, so there is no clear sign that non-significant studies are missing.
  • Bottom line: the visual impression is “some asymmetry, most likely driven by heterogeneity (latitude)”. We check this formally next.

8 Step 6: Egger’s test and friends

Code 
egger <- regtest(res_re, model = "lm", predictor = "sei")  # classic Egger
egger

Regression Test for Funnel Plot Asymmetry

Model:     weighted regression with multiplicative dispersion
Predictor: standard error

Test for Funnel Plot Asymmetry: t = -1.4013, df = 11, p = 0.1887
Limit Estimate (as sei -> 0):   b = -0.1909 (CI: -0.6753, 0.2935)
Code 
ranktest(res_re)

Rank Correlation Test for Funnel Plot Asymmetry

Kendall's tau = 0.0256, p = 0.9524
Code 
res_tf <- trimfill(res_re)
res_tf

Estimated number of missing studies on the right side: 1 (SE = 2.4528)

Random-Effects Model (k = 14; tau^2 estimator: REML)

tau^2 (estimated amount of total heterogeneity): 0.3313 (SE = 0.1701)
tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):      0.5756
I^2 (total heterogeneity / total variability):   92.14%
H^2 (total variability / sampling variability):  12.72

Test for Heterogeneity:
Q(df = 13) = 154.6750, p-val < .0001

Model Results:

estimate      se     zval    pval    ci.lb    ci.ub      
 -0.6571  0.1785  -3.6805  0.0002  -1.0070  -0.3072  *** 

---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
Code 
funnel(res_tf, atransf = exp, legend = TRUE, xlab = "Risk ratio (log scale)")
WarningReading it

How to read the tests: Egger’s test regresses the effect on its standard error. A slope (here t = -1.40) significantly different from 0 means small studies show systematically different results from large ones. Begg’s test asks the same question with rank correlation. How to read the trim-and-fill funnel: open circles are the imputed “missing” studies, mirrored from the opposite side; the vertical line is the adjusted estimate.

What we infer: Egger’s test p = 0.19 and Begg’s test p = 0.95: no strong evidence of small-study effects. Trim-and-fill imputes 1 study on the right side (towards no effect) and moves the pooled RR only from 0.49 to 0.52 (95% CI 0.37 to 0.74). The conclusion that BCG protects is unchanged. Remember:

  • With fewer than 10 studies, do not test for asymmetry (Cochrane Handbook).
  • Asymmetry ≠ publication bias. With I² this high, heterogeneity alone can distort the funnel.
  • Trim-and-fill is a sensitivity analysis, not a correction.

9 Step 7: Leave-one-out sensitivity analysis

Code 
loo <- leave1out(res_re, transf = exp) |>
  tidy_mf() |>
  mutate(study = bcg$study) |>
  select(omitted = study, rr = estimate, ci_lb, ci_ub, I2, tau2)

loo |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))
omitted rr ci_lb ci_ub I2 tau2
Aronson, 1948 0.49 0.34 0.72 93.23 0.34
Ferguson & Simes, 1949 0.52 0.36 0.74 92.25 0.29
Rosenthal et al, 1960 0.50 0.35 0.73 92.94 0.32
Hart & Sutherland, 1977 0.53 0.38 0.75 90.41 0.26
Frimodt-Moller et al, 1973 0.47 0.32 0.68 92.76 0.33
Stein & Aronson, 1953 0.49 0.33 0.73 90.91 0.36
Vandiviere et al, 1973 0.52 0.36 0.74 92.28 0.29
TPT Madras, 1980 0.45 0.32 0.64 87.03 0.27
Coetzee & Berjak, 1968 0.48 0.32 0.70 93.21 0.35
Rosenthal et al, 1961 0.52 0.36 0.75 92.23 0.30
Comstock et al, 1974 0.47 0.32 0.69 91.81 0.34
Comstock & Webster, 1969 0.47 0.33 0.67 92.68 0.31
Comstock et al, 1976 0.46 0.32 0.66 92.34 0.30
Code 
pooled_rr <- exp(res_re$b[1])

loo |>
  mutate(omitted = fct_reorder(omitted, rr)) |>
  ggplot(aes(rr, omitted)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = exp(res_re$ci.lb), xmax = exp(res_re$ci.ub),
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey90") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = pooled_rr, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = ci_lb, xmax = ci_ub)) +
  geom_text(aes(x = ci_ub, label = str_c("I² = ", round(I2), "%")),
            hjust = -0.15, size = 3, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.7, 1),
                expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.25))) +
  labs(x = "Pooled RR when study is omitted (log scale)", y = "Study omitted",
       subtitle = "Dashed line and band = overall pooled RR and 95% CI")
TipHow to read this plot
  • Each row is the meta-analysis re-run without one study (named on the y-axis). The dot is the new pooled RR and the line is its 95% CI.
  • Dashed line and grey band: the original pooled RR and CI with all studies. Red line: RR = 1 (no effect).
  • Rows are sorted by the new pooled RR, so the top and bottom rows are the studies whose removal moves the answer most.
  • Labels on the right show the I² after removal. A big drop marks a study that contributes a lot of heterogeneity.
  • What to look for: does any omission push the estimate outside the grey band, or make the CI cross the red line? If so, the result depends on that one study.
NoteWhat we infer from it
  • Omitting any single trial moves the pooled RR only between 0.45 and 0.53. All dots stay inside the original CI band and every CI stays clear of 1. The conclusion is robust to any one study.
  • TPT Madras (largest trial, null result) is the most influential on the heterogeneity: dropping it lowers I² to 87% and gives the most favourable estimate (0.45).
  • Hart & Sutherland (large, very protective) pulls the other way: dropping it gives the least favourable estimate (0.53).
  • I² stays above 85% whichever study is removed: heterogeneity is not caused by one outlier. It is a feature of the whole evidence base, which is why the meta-regression on latitude matters.

9.1 Influence diagnostics

Code 
inf_re <- influence(res_re)
inf_re |> plot()
TipHow to read this plot

Eight panels, one point per study (x-axis = study number, in the order of the forest plot):

  • rstudent: standardised residual. Values beyond ±2 to 3 mark outliers.
  • dffits and cook.d: how much the pooled estimate changes when the study is removed. Large values mean influential.
  • cov.r: below 1 means removing the study makes the estimate more precise.
  • tau2.del and QE.del: τ² and Q after removing the study. A big drop marks a source of heterogeneity.
  • hat and weight: leverage and weight of each study.
  • Red points are studies flagged as influential by the combined rules of Viechtbauer & Cheung (2010).
NoteWhat we infer from it
  • 0 studies are flagged as influential; no residual exceeds ±2.
  • The highest Cook’s distances belong to Hart & Sutherland (0.23) and TPT Madras (0.20). These two also cause the largest drops in Q (QE.del 97 and 68 vs 152 overall).
  • Together this agrees with leave-one-out: two large trials at opposite extremes drive the heterogeneity, but neither alone changes the conclusion.
Code 
baujat(res_re)
TipHow to read this plot
  • x-axis: how much each study contributes to the overall heterogeneity (its share of Cochran’s Q).
  • y-axis: how much the pooled estimate changes when that study is removed (influence on the result).
  • Top-right corner = studies that both add heterogeneity and move the result. These deserve a closer look (population, design, risk of bias).
  • Bottom-left = studies that agree with the rest and have little leverage.
NoteWhat we infer from it
  • Hart & Sutherland (study 4) and TPT Madras (study 8) sit in the top-right: they are the main drivers of heterogeneity and of the pooled estimate. They lie at opposite latitudes (52° vs 13°), which again points to latitude as the explanation.
  • Comstock & Webster, Vandiviere, Ferguson & Simes, Comstock 1976 and Rosenthal 1961 add heterogeneity but have moderate influence.
  • Stein & Aronson and Aronson sit near the origin: consistent with the pooled result.

11 Appendix: the same analysis with the meta package

The Meta-Analysis with R book (Schwarzer, Carpenter & Rücker, 2015) uses meta. The equivalent calls are below (not run here).

Code 
library(meta)

m <- metabin(
  event.e = tpos, n.e = n_vacc,
  event.c = cpos, n.c = n_ctrl,
  studlab = study, data = bcg,
  sm = "RR", method.tau = "REML",
  common = TRUE, random = TRUE, prediction = TRUE
)

summary(m)                                   # pooled RR, Q, I², τ²
forest(m, sortvar = TE)                      # forest plot
funnel(m, contour = c(0.9, 0.95, 0.99))      # contour-enhanced funnel
metabias(m, method.bias = "Egger")           # Egger's test
trimfill(m)                                  # trim-and-fill
metainf(m, pooled = "random") |> forest()    # leave-one-out
metareg(m, ~ ablat)                          # meta-regression

---
title: "Meta-analysis in R: a worked example"
subtitle: "BCG vaccine and tuberculosis: 13 randomised trials"
author: "Dr Gurpreet"
date: today
format:
  html:
    toc: true

## Why this dataset?

`dat.bcg` (Colditz et al., *Clin Infect Dis* 1994) ships with **metafor**. It has
13 trials of BCG vaccination against tuberculosis, a binary outcome, and a lot
of heterogeneity with a plausible explanation (distance from the equator). That
makes it ideal for teaching every step: pooling, heterogeneity, small-study
effects and sensitivity analysis.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(metafor)
library(tidyverse)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

# Helper: metafor output -> tibble with snake_case names (ci.lb -> ci_lb)
tidy_mf <- \(x) x |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  rename_with(\(nm) str_replace_all(nm, "\\.", "_"))
```

## The data

```{r}
#| label: data
bcg <- dat.bcg |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(
    study  = str_c(author, ", ", year),
    n_vacc = tpos + tneg,
    n_ctrl = cpos + cneg
  ) |>
  select(trial, study, year, ablat, alloc,
         tpos, n_vacc, cpos, n_ctrl, tneg, cneg)

bcg |> select(study, ablat, alloc, tpos, n_vacc, cpos, n_ctrl)
```

`tpos`/`cpos` are TB cases in the vaccinated and control arms; `ablat` is the
absolute latitude of the trial site.

## Step 1: Effect size for each study

`escalc()` computes the **log risk ratio** (`yi`) and its **sampling variance**
(`vi`). We analyse on the log scale and back-transform for reporting.

```{r}
#| label: escalc
bcg_es <- escalc(
  measure = "RR",
  ai = tpos, bi = tneg,   # vaccinated: events, non-events
  ci = cpos, di = cneg,   # control:    events, non-events
  data = bcg,
  slab = study
)

bcg_es |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(
    rr    = exp(yi),
    lower = exp(yi - 1.96 * sqrt(vi)),
    upper = exp(yi + 1.96 * sqrt(vi))
  ) |>
  select(study, yi, vi, rr, lower, upper) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

## Step 2: Pool the studies

```{r}
#| label: models
res_fe <- rma(yi, vi, data = bcg_es, method = "EE")    # common (fixed) effect
res_re <- rma(yi, vi, data = bcg_es, method = "REML")  # random effects

res_re
```

```{r}
#| label: compare-models
pooled <- bind_rows(
  `Common effect`  = predict(res_fe, transf = exp) |> tidy_mf(),
  `Random effects` = predict(res_re, transf = exp) |> tidy_mf(),
  .id = "model"
) |>
  select(model, rr = pred, ci_lb, ci_ub, pi_lb, pi_ub)

pooled |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

```{r}
#| label: inline-numbers
#| include: false
re <- pooled |> filter(model == "Random effects")
f2 <- \(x) format(round(x, 2), nsmall = 2)
pct <- \(x) str_c(round(x, 1), "%")

# Study weights (%) under each model, for the forest-plot discussion
wts <- tibble(
  study = bcg$study,
  w_fe  = weights(res_fe),
  w_re  = weights(res_re)
)
w_madras <- wts |> filter(str_detect(study, "Madras"))
n_cross1 <- bcg_es |>
  as_tibble() |>
  filter(yi + 1.96 * sqrt(vi) > 0) |>
  nrow()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Reading it
Under the random-effects model, BCG vaccination is associated with a pooled
RR of **`r f2(re$rr)`** (95% CI `r f2(re$ci_lb)` to `r f2(re$ci_ub)`), roughly
a `r round(100 * (1 - re$rr))`% reduction in TB risk. The common-effect model
gives a narrower and different answer because it ignores between-study
variation. Here that assumption is clearly wrong (see Step 4).
:::

## Step 3: Forest plot

```{r}
#| label: fig-forest
#| fig-cap: "Forest plot, random-effects model, with 95% prediction interval"
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-width: 10
forest(
  res_re,
  atransf   = exp,
  at        = log(c(0.05, 0.25, 1, 4)),
  xlim      = c(-16, 6),
  ilab      = cbind(bcg$tpos, bcg$n_vacc, bcg$cpos, bcg$n_ctrl),
  ilab.xpos = c(-9.5, -8, -6, -4.5),
  header    = c("Study", "RR [95% CI]"),
  addpred   = TRUE,
  shade     = TRUE,
  mlab      = "Random-effects model (REML)"
)
text(c(-9.5, -8, -6, -4.5), res_re$k + 2, c("TB+", "N", "TB+", "N"), font = 2, cex = 0.8)
text(c(-8.75, -5.25),       res_re$k + 3, c("Vaccinated", "Control"), font = 2, cex = 0.8)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## How to read this plot
* **Each row is one study.** The square is that study's RR; the horizontal
  line is its 95% CI. An arrow means the CI runs off the scale.
* **Square size = weight** in the pooled analysis. Big squares pull the
  diamond towards themselves.
* **Vertical line at RR = 1** is the line of no effect. Left of it favours
  vaccination (fewer TB cases); right of it favours control.
* **The diamond** is the pooled RR: its centre is the point estimate and its
  width is the 95% CI.
* **The dotted line through the diamond** is the 95% **prediction interval**:
  the range in which the true effect of a *new* similar study is expected to
  lie.
* **The x-axis is logarithmic**, so RR 0.5 and RR 2 are equally far from 1.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What we infer from it
* **Direction:** `r res_re$k - 2` of `r res_re$k` trials lie left of 1; only
  TPT Madras (RR 1.01) and Comstock & Webster (RR 1.56) do not.
* **Precision varies:** `r n_cross1` trials have a CI that crosses 1 on their
  own, yet the pooled diamond (`r f2(re$rr)`, `r f2(re$ci_lb)` to
  `r f2(re$ci_ub)`) sits clearly left of 1. Pooling gives a precise answer
  that no single small trial could.
* **Visible heterogeneity (eyeball test):** many CIs do not overlap each other
  (e.g. Hart & Sutherland 0.24 vs TPT Madras 1.01). Studies are not estimating
  one common effect.
* **Weights are fairly even** (`r f2(min(wts$w_re))`% to
  `r f2(max(wts$w_re))`%) because τ² is large. Under a common-effect model
  TPT Madras alone would carry `r f2(w_madras$w_fe)`% of the weight, versus
  `r f2(w_madras$w_re)`% here.
* **Prediction interval crosses 1** (`r f2(re$pi_lb)` to `r f2(re$pi_ub)`):
  BCG works *on average*, but in some settings it may give little or no
  protection. Report both the CI and the PI.
:::

## Step 4: Heterogeneity

```{r}
#| label: heterogeneity
tibble(
  statistic = c("Q", "df", "p (Q)", "tau^2", "tau", "I^2 (%)", "H^2"),
  value     = c(res_re$QE, res_re$k - 1, res_re$QEp,
                res_re$tau2, sqrt(res_re$tau2), res_re$I2, res_re$H2)
) |>
  mutate(value = if_else(statistic == "p (Q)",
                         format.pval(value, eps = 1e-4),
                         as.character(round(value, 2))))
```

Confidence intervals for the heterogeneity parameters:

```{r}
#| label: het-ci
confint(res_re)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Reading it
* **Q test**: rejects homogeneity (p < 0.0001), but it has low power with few
  studies and too much power with many, so do not rely on it alone.
* **I² = `r round(res_re$I2)`%**: the share of total variability due to real
  differences between studies, not chance. It is a *proportion*, not an
  absolute amount.
* **τ² = `r f2(res_re$tau2)`**: the *absolute* between-study variance on the
  log RR scale.
* **Prediction interval `r f2(re$pi_lb)` to `r f2(re$pi_ub)`**: a new trial
  in a new setting could plausibly find anything from a large benefit to no
  benefit or even harm. This is often the most useful number for clinicians.
:::

### Explaining heterogeneity: meta-regression on latitude

```{r}
#| label: metareg
res_mr <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ ablat, data = bcg_es, method = "REML")
res_mr
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-bubble
#| fig-cap: "Bubble plot: BCG efficacy improves further from the equator"
lat_grid <- tibble(ablat = seq(10, 60, by = 1))

lat_pred <- predict(res_mr, newmods = lat_grid$ablat, transf = exp) |>
  tidy_mf() |>
  bind_cols(lat_grid)

bcg_es |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(rr = exp(yi), weight = 1 / vi) |>
  ggplot(aes(ablat, rr)) +
  geom_ribbon(data = lat_pred, aes(y = pred, ymin = ci_lb, ymax = ci_ub),
              fill = "grey85") +
  geom_line(data = lat_pred, aes(y = pred), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(size = weight), shape = 21, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 12, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Absolute latitude (degrees)", y = "Risk ratio (log scale)",
       subtitle = "Point size proportional to inverse-variance weight")
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## How to read this plot
* **Each bubble is one trial**, placed at its latitude (x) and its RR (y,
  log scale). **Bubble size = weight** in the meta-regression.
* **The solid line** is the fitted meta-regression; **the grey band** is its
  95% CI.
* **Dashed line at RR = 1** is no effect. Where the band sits below it, the
  model predicts a protective effect.
* A sloping line means the moderator explains part of the heterogeneity; a
  flat line means it does not.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What we infer from it
* **Clear dose-response with latitude:** each extra degree from the equator
  multiplies the RR by `r f2(exp(res_mr$b[2]))`, i.e. about
  `r round(100 * (1 - exp(res_mr$b[2])), 1)`% more protection per degree
  (p `r if (res_mr$QMp < 1e-4) "< 0.0001" else str_c("= ", f2(res_mr$QMp))`).
* **Near the equator BCG shows little effect** (trials at 13-19°, such as TPT
  Madras and Frimodt-Moller, sit near RR = 1). **Far from the equator it is
  highly protective** (RR around 0.2-0.3 above 50°).
* Latitude explains about **`r round(res_mr$R2)`%** of the between-study
  variance (R²), and residual I² falls from `r round(res_re$I2)`% to
  `r round(res_mr$I2)`%. Heterogeneity is largely *explained*, not just
  noise.
* **Caution:** this is an observational association *across* studies
  (ecological). Latitude is a proxy for something else, plausibly prior
  exposure to environmental mycobacteria. With 13 studies, one moderator is
  the most the data can support (about 10 studies per covariate).
:::

## Step 5: Funnel plot

```{r}
#| label: fig-funnel
#| fig-cap: "Funnel plot (left) and contour-enhanced funnel plot (right)"
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
funnel(res_re, atransf = exp, xlab = "Risk ratio (log scale)")
funnel(res_re, level = c(90, 95, 99),
       shade = c("white", "grey80", "grey60"),
       refline = 0, legend = TRUE,
       atransf = exp, xlab = "Risk ratio (log scale)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## How to read this plot
* **x-axis:** each study's effect (RR, log scale). **y-axis:** its standard
  error, *inverted*, so large precise studies are at the top and small
  imprecise ones at the bottom.
* **Vertical line:** the pooled estimate. **Triangle (left panel):** where
  95% of studies should fall if there were no bias and no heterogeneity.
* **Expected shape:** a symmetrical inverted funnel. Big studies cluster
  tightly near the top; small studies scatter widely but *evenly on both
  sides* at the bottom.
* **Asymmetry** (a gap in one bottom corner) suggests small studies with
  "unfavourable" results are missing.
* **Contour-enhanced panel (right):** the reference line is RR = 1 and the
  shading marks where results are statistically significant (grey zones:
  p < 0.10, < 0.05, < 0.01). If the gap is in the white (non-significant)
  zone, publication bias is a plausible cause. If it is in a significant
  zone, look for other causes (heterogeneity, small-trial quality, chance).
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What we infer from it
* **The large trials** (TPT Madras, Stein & Aronson, Comstock 1974, Hart &
  Sutherland) sit at the top but are **spread widely left to right**. That
  spread among precise studies is heterogeneity, not publication bias.
* **Many points fall outside the triangle.** Expected when I² is
  `r round(res_re$I2)`%: the triangle assumes a single common effect.
* **Small trials at the bottom mostly lie to the left** (strong benefit), with
  one on the right (Comstock & Webster, RR 1.56). There is only a mild hint of
  asymmetry.
* **In the contour panel**, the small trials sit in both shaded and white
  zones, so there is no clear sign that non-significant studies are missing.
* **Bottom line:** the visual impression is "some asymmetry, most likely
  driven by heterogeneity (latitude)". We check this formally next.
:::

## Step 6: Egger's test and friends

```{r}
#| label: egger
egger <- regtest(res_re, model = "lm", predictor = "sei")  # classic Egger
egger
```

```{r}
#| label: begg
ranktest(res_re)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-trimfill
#| fig-cap: "Trim-and-fill: imputed study shown as an open circle"
res_tf <- trimfill(res_re)
res_tf
funnel(res_tf, atransf = exp, legend = TRUE, xlab = "Risk ratio (log scale)")
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Reading it
**How to read the tests:** Egger's test regresses the effect on its standard
error. A slope (here t = `r f2(egger$zval)`) significantly different from 0
means small studies show systematically different results from large ones.
Begg's test asks the same question with rank correlation. **How to read the
trim-and-fill funnel:** open circles are the *imputed* "missing" studies,
mirrored from the opposite side; the vertical line is the adjusted estimate.

**What we infer:** Egger's test p = `r f2(egger$pval)` and Begg's test
p = `r f2(ranktest(res_re)$pval)`: no strong evidence of small-study effects.
Trim-and-fill imputes `r res_tf$k0` study on the `r res_tf$side` side (towards
no effect) and moves the pooled RR only from `r f2(re$rr)` to
`r f2(exp(res_tf$b[1]))` (95% CI `r f2(exp(res_tf$ci.lb))` to
`r f2(exp(res_tf$ci.ub))`). The conclusion that BCG protects is unchanged.
Remember:

* With fewer than 10 studies, do not test for asymmetry (Cochrane Handbook).
* Asymmetry ≠ publication bias. With I² this high, heterogeneity alone can
  distort the funnel.
* Trim-and-fill is a sensitivity analysis, not a correction.
:::

## Step 7: Leave-one-out sensitivity analysis

```{r}
#| label: loo
loo <- leave1out(res_re, transf = exp) |>
  tidy_mf() |>
  mutate(study = bcg$study) |>
  select(omitted = study, rr = estimate, ci_lb, ci_ub, I2, tau2)

loo |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-loo
#| fig-cap: "Pooled RR after omitting each study in turn"
pooled_rr <- exp(res_re$b[1])

loo |>
  mutate(omitted = fct_reorder(omitted, rr)) |>
  ggplot(aes(rr, omitted)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = exp(res_re$ci.lb), xmax = exp(res_re$ci.ub),
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey90") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = pooled_rr, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = ci_lb, xmax = ci_ub)) +
  geom_text(aes(x = ci_ub, label = str_c("I² = ", round(I2), "%")),
            hjust = -0.15, size = 3, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.7, 1),
                expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.25))) +
  labs(x = "Pooled RR when study is omitted (log scale)", y = "Study omitted",
       subtitle = "Dashed line and band = overall pooled RR and 95% CI")
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## How to read this plot
* **Each row is the meta-analysis re-run without one study** (named on the
  y-axis). The dot is the new pooled RR and the line is its 95% CI.
* **Dashed line and grey band:** the original pooled RR and CI with all
  studies. **Red line:** RR = 1 (no effect).
* **Rows are sorted** by the new pooled RR, so the top and bottom rows are the
  studies whose removal moves the answer most.
* **Labels on the right** show the I² after removal. A big drop marks a study
  that contributes a lot of heterogeneity.
* **What to look for:** does any omission push the estimate outside the grey
  band, or make the CI cross the red line? If so, the result depends on that
  one study.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What we infer from it
* Omitting any single trial moves the pooled RR only between
  `r f2(min(loo$rr))` and `r f2(max(loo$rr))`. All dots stay inside the
  original CI band and **every CI stays clear of 1**. The conclusion is
  **robust** to any one study.
* **TPT Madras** (largest trial, null result) is the most influential on the
  *heterogeneity*: dropping it lowers I² to
  `r round(loo$I2[str_detect(loo$omitted, "Madras")])`% and gives the most
  favourable estimate (`r f2(loo$rr[str_detect(loo$omitted, "Madras")])`).
* **Hart & Sutherland** (large, very protective) pulls the other way: dropping
  it gives the least favourable estimate
  (`r f2(loo$rr[str_detect(loo$omitted, "Hart")])`).
* **I² stays above 85% whichever study is removed:** heterogeneity is not
  caused by one outlier. It is a feature of the whole evidence base, which is
  why the meta-regression on latitude matters.
:::

### Influence diagnostics

```{r}
#| label: fig-influence
#| fig-cap: "Influence diagnostics (Viechtbauer & Cheung, 2010)"
#| fig-height: 8
inf_re <- influence(res_re)
inf_re |> plot()
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## How to read this plot
Eight panels, one point per study (x-axis = study number, in the order of the
forest plot):

* **rstudent:** standardised residual. Values beyond ±2 to 3 mark outliers.
* **dffits** and **cook.d:** how much the pooled estimate changes when the
  study is removed. Large values mean influential.
* **cov.r:** below 1 means removing the study makes the estimate *more*
  precise.
* **tau2.del** and **QE.del:** τ² and Q after removing the study. A big drop
  marks a source of heterogeneity.
* **hat** and **weight:** leverage and weight of each study.
* **Red points** are studies flagged as influential by the combined rules of
  Viechtbauer & Cheung (2010).
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What we infer from it
* **`r sum(inf_re$is.infl)` studies are flagged as influential**; no residual
  exceeds ±2.
* The highest Cook's distances belong to **Hart & Sutherland**
  (`r f2(inf_re$inf$cook.d[4])`) and **TPT Madras**
  (`r f2(inf_re$inf$cook.d[8])`). These two also cause the largest drops in Q
  (QE.del `r round(inf_re$inf$QE.del[4])` and
  `r round(inf_re$inf$QE.del[8])` vs `r round(res_re$QE)` overall).
* Together this agrees with leave-one-out: two large trials at opposite
  extremes drive the heterogeneity, but neither alone changes the conclusion.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-baujat
#| fig-cap: "Baujat plot: contribution to heterogeneity (x) vs influence on the pooled result (y)"
baujat(res_re)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## How to read this plot
* **x-axis:** how much each study contributes to the overall heterogeneity
  (its share of Cochran's Q).
* **y-axis:** how much the pooled estimate changes when that study is
  removed (influence on the result).
* **Top-right corner** = studies that both add heterogeneity *and* move the
  result. These deserve a closer look (population, design, risk of bias).
* **Bottom-left** = studies that agree with the rest and have little
  leverage.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What we infer from it
* **Hart & Sutherland (study 4)** and **TPT Madras (study 8)** sit in the
  top-right: they are the main drivers of heterogeneity and of the pooled
  estimate. They lie at opposite latitudes (52° vs 13°), which again points to
  latitude as the explanation.
* **Comstock & Webster, Vandiviere, Ferguson & Simes, Comstock 1976 and
  Rosenthal 1961** add
  heterogeneity but have moderate influence.
* **Stein & Aronson and Aronson** sit near the origin: consistent with the
  pooled result.
:::

## Summary for the slide

```{r}
#| label: summary
tibble(
  item = c("Studies (k)", "Pooled RR (RE, 95% CI)", "95% prediction interval",
           "I²", "τ²", "Egger p", "Leave-one-out RR range"),
  result = c(
    res_re$k,
    str_glue("{f2(re$rr)} ({f2(re$ci_lb)} to {f2(re$ci_ub)})"),
    str_glue("{f2(re$pi_lb)} to {f2(re$pi_ub)}"),
    str_c(round(res_re$I2), "%"),
    f2(res_re$tau2),
    f2(egger$pval),
    str_glue("{f2(min(loo$rr))} to {f2(max(loo$rr))}")
  )
)
```

## Appendix: the same analysis with the **meta** package

The *Meta-Analysis with R* book (Schwarzer, Carpenter & Rücker, 2015) uses
**meta**. The equivalent calls are below (not run here).

```{r}
#| label: meta-pkg
#| eval: false
library(meta)

m <- metabin(
  event.e = tpos, n.e = n_vacc,
  event.c = cpos, n.c = n_ctrl,
  studlab = study, data = bcg,
  sm = "RR", method.tau = "REML",
  common = TRUE, random = TRUE, prediction = TRUE
)

summary(m)                                   # pooled RR, Q, I², τ²
forest(m, sortvar = TE)                      # forest plot
funnel(m, contour = c(0.9, 0.95, 0.99))      # contour-enhanced funnel
metabias(m, method.bias = "Egger")           # Egger's test
trimfill(m)                                  # trim-and-fill
metainf(m, pooled = "random") |> forest()    # leave-one-out
metareg(m, ~ ablat)                          # meta-regression
```
